title: The Bakery: Real Bread
strapline: Warm flour, sticky dough and a loaf that rises while you watch — the oldest kitchen science there is.
intent: Making real bread lets children feel a material transform completely under their own hands — powdery flour becomes a sticky mass, then a springy dough, then something warm and golden they can eat.
Kneading is deeply satisfying, whole-arm work that builds hand strength and lets a busy child pour effort into something that visibly improves.
Bread follows a genuine sequence with a real wait — mix, knead, prove, bake — so children hold a goal in mind across time and learn that good things are worth waiting for.
Watching dough rise in a warm bowl raises honest questions about change and living yeast that children keep coming back to.
Bread belongs to every family and every culture, so the bakery welcomes flatbreads, chapatis, challah and rolls from the homes in the room.
implementation: Weigh and mix together at the children's pace, letting them tip, stir and get their hands right into the bowl even when it is slower and messier.
Make kneading a shared, unhurried job — push, fold, turn — and let each child take the dough somewhere private to work it hard.
Photograph the proving bowl every ten minutes and line the pictures up afterwards so children can see and retell the rising for themselves.
Wonder aloud rather than explain: 'it was this big, now look — where did all that air come from?'
Bring in family breads, ideally with a parent baking their own recipe alongside the children, and taste widely at the end.
Close the loop by eating the warm loaf together at snack, buttered, with the whole room invited to try what the bakers made.
key_questions: It was this big — now look! Where did all that air come from?
How does the flour feel now we've added the water?
What do we need to do first, and what comes next?
How many rolls have we shaped? Is that enough for everyone?
What bread does your family make at home?

impact.text: Children plant, mix and bake, watching a material change completely under the heat.
Children knead, shape and handle dough, building whole-arm strength and one-handed control.
Children hold a goal in mind across a real wait — mix, knead, prove, bake — and see it through.
Children count and compare as they bake — how many rolls, enough for everyone, weighing the flour.
Children meet the breads of many families and value their own home's bread being made here.

enhancements: A photo sequence of the proving bowl every ten minutes, lined up so children retell the rising.
A family-breads week — chapati, challah, flatbread — ideally baked by a parent alongside the children.
A role-play bakery with tills, price labels and paper bags once the real loaf is done.
Grinding a few wheat grains to connect the flour to the field.
Buttering and sharing the warm loaf at snack with the whole room invited to taste.

playing_exploring: Flour and dough are irresistible to handle, and this material has the rare bonus of becoming food.
Children test what their hands can do — poke a hole, stretch it thin, roll a snake, squash it flat.
active_learning: Kneading is effortful, absorbing work with a clear finish, and children stick with it because the dough rewards them.
Waiting through the prove and the bake, then finding it worth it, is patience made delicious.
creating_thinking: Children predict what the oven's heat will do and watch their guess meet the risen, golden reality.
A flat, heavy loaf invites the real question — what did we forget, and what shall we try next time?
